slide.title: Final Checks Before Class
slide.body: A folder with six document icons and a checklist with four teal ticks. Small tag: AI for Educators and Trainers · Lesson 12 · Capstone step 4.

scenes.on_screen_text: Safe and fair for real learners
scenes.voiceover: Your unit now has a plan, a quiz and a rubric. The last step is the one that makes it safe and fair to use with real learners. You put all the pieces together, and review them as a whole, with the eyes of a careful colleague.

slide.title: Your unit pack: six parts
slide.body: 1. Unit plan + 2 full lesson plans (L11) · 2. Differentiated materials (L06) · 3. Accessible visual (L07) · 4. Quiz (L09) · 5. Rubric (L10) · 6. Unit AI policy (L04)

scenes.voiceover: In this final lesson, you complete your unit pack and review it. The pack has six parts. Your unit plan, with at least two full lesson plans. Differentiated materials in support, core and challenge versions. One accessible visual material. Your quiz. The rubric for your main task. And a unit AI policy, using the traffic-light model.

slide.title: Final review: four areas
slide.body: Four quadrants: Accuracy · Bias and representation · Accessibility · Alignment. First two highlighted.

scenes.voiceover: Then you run a final review in four areas. Accuracy: check every fact and answer key against a reliable source. Bias and representation: look across the whole pack. Does one group appear again and again in the same role?

slide.title: Final review: four areas
slide.body: Same quadrants; Accessibility and Alignment highlighted. Padlock banner across the bottom: no learner names, grades or personal data anywhere.

scenes.voiceover: Accessibility: clear fonts, contrast, alt text, simple layout, plain instructions, and suitable reading levels, including for second-language learners. And alignment: every outcome is taught, practised and assessed, and every activity supports an outcome. One more check. Make sure no learner names, grades or personal data appear anywhere in the pack.

slide.title: Your AI-use note
slide.body: Table: Part | How AI helped | What I changed. Example row: Quiz | drafted 12 questions | removed 3, rewrote 4 wrong options.

scenes.voiceover: Last, write a short AI-use note. It tells a reader where you used AI, what you checked, and what you changed. It is the same honesty you ask of learners in an amber task. A simple table works well.

scenes.stock_query: pilot going through checklist in cockpit
scenes.on_screen_text: The checklist catches what you miss
scenes.voiceover: The final review is like a pilot's checklist before take-off. The pilot knows how to fly, but the checklist catches the small thing that is easy to miss when you are busy. Your checklists do the same for facts, fairness and access.

scenes.stock_query: adult students training as tour guides
scenes.voiceover: Let's see a final review. Rosa teaches at a technical institute in Cusco, in Peru. Her unit, Responsible Tourism, has four lessons for adult students training to become tour guides. She collects all six parts in one shared folder, and then she reviews.

slide.title: Accuracy
slide.body: Before: a specific visitor number (blurred, question mark: not confirmed). After: a general statement. Rule: cannot confirm it → remove it.

scenes.voiceover: Accuracy first. One reading text, drafted with AI, gives a visitor number for a local site. She cannot confirm it in an official source, so she removes the number, and uses a general statement instead.

slide.title: Bias across the pack
slide.body: Before: tourists only from Europe and North America; locals only sellers. After: a tourist from Brazil · a group from Japan · a local guide who runs a business.

scenes.voiceover: Then bias. Across the pack, every tourist in her examples is from Europe or North America, and every local person is a seller. So she changes several examples. A tourist from Brazil, a group from Japan, and a local guide who manages a business.

slide.title: Accessibility
slide.body: Before: green and red boxes only. After: green box with a tick, red box with a cross. Plus: alt text added to two photos.

scenes.voiceover: Accessibility. Her infographic uses green and red to show good and bad practice. She adds a tick and a cross, because colour alone does not work for every learner. She also adds alt text to two photos she had missed.

slide.title: Alignment and AI-use note
slide.body: 'Handling a difficult visitor': taught in lesson 3, missing from rubric → criterion added · AI-use note: part · how AI helped · what she changed

scenes.voiceover: And alignment. Her outcome on handling a difficult visitor is taught in lesson three, but it is not in the rubric. So she adds a criterion. Her AI-use note then records each part, how AI helped, and what she changed. For example, AI drafted twelve quiz questions, and she removed three and rewrote four wrong options.

scenes.on_screen_text: Review the whole pack, in order
scenes.voiceover: A common mistake is to review each part separately, and never look at the pack as a whole. Some problems only appear across the unit, like one kind of person always in the same role, or a policy that marks a task red while a lesson plan tells learners to use AI for it. Read the whole pack in order, as a learner would. And make your AI-use note specific.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Six parts: plan · materials · visual · quiz · rubric · policy. 2. Review the whole pack: accuracy, bias, access, alignment. 3. Specific AI-use note.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, the unit pack has six parts: the unit plan, differentiated materials, an accessible visual, the quiz, the rubric and a unit AI policy. Second, review the whole pack for accuracy, bias, accessibility and alignment, not only each part alone. Third, a short, specific AI-use note shows where AI helped, and what you checked and changed.

Congratulations. You have reached the end of AI for Educators and Trainers. Your last step is step four of the capstone. Complete your unit pack, review it with the checklists from lessons seven and eight, and write your AI-use note. Then submit your unit for assessment. Thank you for learning with us, and enjoy using your unit with real learners.
